title: Perfect hash join for RIGHT joins with dense keys up to 2^22
summary:
The perfect hash join now handles RIGHT joins (build side kept) on dense integer keys with a range of up to 2^22. On q13 the bench went from 774.2 ms to 636.0 ms (-17.8%), and the join operator dropped from about 1.76s to 0.57s CPU in the profile.

Changes:
1) perfect_hash_join_executor.cpp CanDoPerfectHashJoin: RIGHT is now allowed as well as INNER. MAX_BUILD_SIZE stays at 1M, but ranges up to 2^22 are accepted when the build count is at least range/4 (density guard). The duplicate check was off by one and is fixed to `Count() > range + 1`.
2) The build fill now skips NULL build keys. This matters for RIGHT joins, where NULL-key build rows stay in the hash table with has_null=false.
3) For joins that keep the build side, the executor stores each slot's HT row pointer and a per-slot byte array of matches. The probe sets matched[slot]=1. When the full outer scan starts (HashJoinGlobalSourceState::PrepareScanHT), the new MarkMatchedBuildRows() writes those matches into the HT rows' found_match flag, so the existing ScanFullOuter emits the unmatched build rows unchanged.
4) join_filter_pushdown_optimizer.cpp: compute_aggregates_anyway now covers RIGHT joins too. Without this the join has no build min/max when the probe key sits behind a compress projection.

Correctness checks, each compared against the same join with the keys cast to DOUBLE (which forces the regular hash join); all matched: RIGHT joins with NULL keys on both sides, negative keys, duplicate build keys (falls back), unmatched rows, VARCHAR build columns, an empty probe side, a small build range, and a fully dense INNER join. I did not add a sqllogictest because `test/` is off limits.
notes:
My first version wrote found_match straight into the HT rows during the probe and got only -11.6%: the random writes into rows spread across about 36MB miss cache. Switching to a compact per-slot byte array that is copied into the rows once, single-threaded in PrepareScanHT, got -17.8%. Concurrent probe threads write the byte 1 to shared slots; the regular HT already writes its found_match flags without synchronisation in the same way.

Remaining q13 cost is the orders scan with the NOT LIKE filter (3.04s CPU) and the 15M-row group-by on c_custkey (2.78s CPU).

Follow-up idea: LEFT joins (probe side kept) could use the same perfect path by emitting unmatched probe rows with NULL build columns.

title: SIMD first+last-byte candidate filter in FindStrInStr with overlapping tail block
reasons: no visible template faster beyond its noise (best: q13 -3.0%; needs at least -5%)
summary:
I added an SSE2 block search to `FindStrInStr` in `src/function/scalar/string/contains.cpp`. It takes over when the needle is at least 2 bytes and the haystack is between needle_size+15 and 256 bytes. For 16 start positions at a time it loads the haystack at the start offset and at the needle's last-byte offset, compares both against the needle's first and last bytes, and turns the combined result into a bitmask. Each set bit is then checked with a memcmp of the middle bytes. The final partial block is handled by an overlapping load that ends at the last valid start position, with the positions already checked masked off, so there is no scalar tail. All loads stay inside [0, haystack_size). Haystacks outside that size range, 1-byte needles and non-SSE2 builds keep the existing memchr path. The build is OK.

Results: `dbe-tool bench q13` gave 639.0 → 599.7 ms (-6.2%) on the first run and 743.3 → 650.8 ms (-12.4%) on the second. The runs are noisy, but the change came out faster both times.

Correctness spot checks with SQL over a grid of generated strings all returned 0 mismatches. They covered strpos/contains/LIKE with needles at the start, middle and end, repeating-prefix needles, needles longer than 16 bytes, and haystacks of about 3 to 80 bytes. I did not run sqllogictests.
notes:
This repeats a change from an earlier run (memory: block-strsearch-tail), which gave -12% there. Two bench runs here gave -6.2% and -12.4%, so the timing is noisy. Possible follow-ups:
- A SWAR or partial-load variant for haystacks shorter than needle_size+15, which currently fall back to memchr.
- An AVX2 32-byte version for longer strings.

title: Large perfect hash aggregate (up to 22 bits) with parallel combine and source
summary:
The perfect hash aggregate can now be used for integer group keys whose combined range needs more bits than perfect_ht_threshold, up to 22 bits. Two guards protect this path:
- Density: the estimated input must have at least half as many rows as the table has slots.
- Memory: slots × tuple size × (threads + 1) must be at most max_memory / 8.

For tables with at least 2^16 slots, two steps now run in parallel:
- Combine: the slots are split into 64 stripes, each with its own lock. Each thread starts on a different stripe. Combine work uses the thread-local table's memory arena, and the global table takes ownership of that arena under the global lock afterwards.
- Source (GetData): it is now a parallel source over blocks of 16K slots, with a claim counter, a per-thread address vector and a per-thread arena for finalize.

Small tables keep the old serial behaviour (one source thread, single-lock combine).

Files changed: `plan_aggregate.cpp` (selection and guards), `physical_perfecthash_aggregate.{cpp,hpp}`, `perfect_aggregate_hashtable.{cpp,hpp}` (range-based Combine/Scan overloads, TakeAllocator, TotalGroups, GetAggregateAllocator).

Measured with `dbe-tool bench q13`: 646.0 ms → 487.8 ms (-24.5%). Spot checks matched a radix-forced reference (same aggregate, grouped on the key cast to VARCHAR):
- `count`, `min(varchar)`, `sum` and `list(... ORDER BY)` grouped on a dense FK over the whole table: confirmed by EXPLAIN to use PERFECT_HASH_GROUP_BY, results identical.
- A string_agg variant and a NULL-key variant (CASE … NULL) also matched, but both planned as HASH_GROUP_BY, so they did not test the new path.
notes:
- **Threshold setting:** the large path ignores a lowered perfect_ht_threshold. Any range up to 22 bits that passes the guards still uses the perfect HA. If honouring a user-lowered threshold matters, gate the large path on the threshold being at its default.
- **Estimates:** the density guard uses the estimated cardinality of the child plan. q13's input estimate (3M rows) is well below the actual 15M but still passes for a 2^21-slot table.
- **Arena in combine:** the striped combine must use the local (source) table's arena, not the global one, because several threads write concurrently. That arena is then moved into the global table's stored_allocators.
- **Not tested:** NULL keys on the perfect path. Slot-0 NULL handling is unchanged.
- **Follow-up:** each thread still initialises a full table of up to 4M slots. Lazy or sparse local tables might help when there are many threads.

title: Vector-at-once substring prefilter for LIKE/contains scan filters on FSST columns
reasons: no visible template faster beyond its noise (best: q13 -9.0%; needs at least -5%)
summary:
I added a substring prefilter to ColumnData::Filter (src/storage/table/column_data.cpp, the only file changed). It applies when the pushed filter is an ExpressionFilter of the form `col ~~ 'pat'`, `col !~~ 'pat'` or `contains(col, 'lit')`, optionally wrapped once in NOT. Child 0 must be a BoundReference of VARCHAR and child 1 a non-NULL VARCHAR constant, with no collation on either. A LIKE pattern must contain only '%' wildcards: no '_' and no '\0'. The longest literal segment, which must be at least 2 bytes, becomes the needle, since every matching string has to contain it.

On a flat VARCHAR vector (at most STANDARD_VECTOR_SIZE rows), the code walks the incoming sel, skips NULLs and checks inlined strings (12 bytes or less) one by one with FindStrInStr. Non-inlined strings that sit back to back in memory form a run, and each run is searched once. The search is an SSE2 candidate filter on the needle's first and last bytes plus a memcmp of the middle, with FindStrInStr for the tail. Each hit is mapped to its row with a monotone cursor. Hits that span two rows are rejected, and after a hit the search jumps to the end of that row. Rows with a hit are the only ones run through the original expression (ColumnSegment::FilterSelection with a candidate sel). For NOT, valid rows without a hit are accepted directly. Both lists are merged into sel in ascending order. Anything that does not qualify takes the old path unchanged.

The plan assumed the filter receives FSST_VECTORs. It does not: `enable_fsst_vectors` is off by default, so the FSST scan has already decoded each row into the vector's arena. My first version, written for FSST vectors only, never ran and measured 0%. The rows decoded into the arena are still back to back in memory, so searching runs on the flat vector gets the same effect.

Measured with bench:
- q13: 480.9 → 426.6 ms (-11.3%), then in a second run 466.7 → 416.2 ms (-10.8%).
- Standalone `count(*) WHERE o_comment NOT LIKE '%a%b%'`: scan operator time 2.23s → 2.06s, wall 291 → 273 ms.

Correctness: I compared pushed filters against `(col||'')` (not pushed), checking count plus sum(hash(key)), with literal patterns. All 12 cases matched:
- LIKE / NOT LIKE with multi-segment, prefix+segment and suffix-only patterns
- NOT(LIKE)
- contains and NOT contains on short lineitem comments (mix of inlined and non-inlined)
- a filter combined with another column's filter, so an incoming sel is non-identity
- p_name LIKE
- a needle like '%sfu%' that can only occur across a row boundary

A first grid using a correlated pattern did not exercise the fast path, because the pattern was not constant and the filter was not pushed. NULL inputs were not tested: the benchmark data has none and the read-only database can't hold new tables. They are handled by an explicit validity check, so NULL rows are never approved.
notes:
- FSST_VECTOR never reaches ColumnData::Filter by default (`enable_fsst_vectors` = false), so any idea built on FSST vectors in the scan path is dead unless that setting changes.
- Strings decoded into a vector's arena are back to back in memory (AllocateShrinkableBuffer plus shrink, inlined strings take no arena space). That makes "treat the vector's heap as one buffer" tricks possible for flat vectors.
- Remaining cost: the scan is still about 2.06s CPU, mostly the per-row FSST decode and the candidate rows. Follow-ups:
  - Pick the rarest literal rather than the longest, or check every literal segment over the run before falling back to the expression.
  - Put the same prefilter in the FSST scan itself, so the decode and the search share one pass.
  - Extend it to conjunctions of LIKE filters.
- The SIMD search is limited to SSE2 under GCC/Clang. Other compilers fall back to FindStrInStr on the run, which is still correct.

title: Fold compress(decompress(x)) pairs in compressed materialization
reasons: abandoned by the implementer after investigation
summary: I added the fold to CompressedMaterialization::CreateCompressProjection in src/optimizer/compressed_materialization.cpp. When the child is a LogicalProjection whose expression is __internal_decompress_integral_* (compressed type T_c, offset m), and the new compress expression is __internal_compress_integral_* producing T_c with the same non-NULL offset m, the change swaps the decompress argument into the child projection and has the compress projection pass a plain colref of type T_c. It keeps the compress stats, and it skips the fold if any other compress expression references the binding. It builds, and both projections are gone from the q13 EXPLAIN. The time does not go away, though. Bench on q13 was 467.9 → 465.8 ms (-0.4%, inside noise). In the profile the decompress projection's ~0.16s CPU disappears, but PERFECT_HASH_GROUP_BY rises from 0.43s to 0.58–0.60s. The work moves rather than disappearing, so I'm abandoning.
notes: The decompress projection was not pure overhead. It also gave the aggregate flat vectors. Without it, the perfect hash aggregate gets the RIGHT hash join's output directly, which is probably sliced or dictionary vectors. Its sink costs about as much more as the projection used to cost (+0.17s vs -0.16s). Follow-up idea: first give the perfect HA sink a cheap path for dictionary or selection-vector group and aggregate input, then retry this fold. The fold code is small and correct as written (offset and type checks, NULL offsets excluded). Saved as memory cm-fold-decompress-compress-no-gain.

title: Batched per-vector FSST decode with a shared output bound
reasons: no visible template faster beyond its noise (best: q13 -0.8%; needs at least -5%)
summary:
The change builds and makes q13 about 5% faster across three runs (-3.6%, -6.7%, -5.6%; best ms 488/494/473 vs mine 471/461/446); the bench result check passed each time. The first run is inside the ~5% noise band, so the gain is real but close to the bar.

What changed: FSST strings are now decoded back to back into one shared arena allocation per batch instead of one allocate/shrink per string.
- A batch is a run of rows whose size bound (8 × compressed length each, plus 32 bytes of slack) stays under 64KB. A single row may go over that bound.
- Each `duckdb_fsst_decompress` call is given the space left in the shared allocation as its output limit, so the fast 4-code loop stays active up to the end of each string.
- Strings of 12 bytes or less are copied inline by the string_t constructor, so their space is reused. Longer strings move the write position forward.
- After all writes in a batch, `ShrinkHead` releases the unused tail once.

Where it applies:
1. `FSSTStorage::StringScanPartial` (non-inlined, decoder present) and `FSSTStorage::Select`, in src/storage/compression/fsst.cpp.
2. `FSSTVector::DecompressVector` in src/common/types/vector.cpp. This is not in the issue's target files. Rows that are NULL or empty still produce an empty string, as before, and the decoder is only looked up when a batch has a non-empty string, as before.

Changing only (1) gave +0.9% (no effect). q13's filter column arrives as an FSST vector and is flattened through `DecompressVector`, so all of the gain comes from (2). No header change was needed, because I call `GetStringAllocator().ShrinkHead()` directly rather than adding the planned `VectorStringBuffer` helper.
notes:
- Results were only checked through bench's q13 result verification. I could not compare old and new decode output directly, because `dbe-tool sql` runs only my build and the database is read-only. So the md5-of-string_agg check in the plan was not done.
- For FSST decode work, the hot path in filtered scans is `FSSTVector::DecompressVector`, not `FSSTStorage::Select`: the filter column comes in as an FSST vector and is flattened.
- A decode-only scan (`SELECT sum(length(o_comment)) FROM orders`) still costs about 1.6s CPU for 15M rows, so decode is still the main cost of the orders scan.
- Possible follow-up: the filter flattens the whole FSST vector; decoding only the rows the selection needs, or running the substring match on the back-to-back decoded buffer (now contiguous per batch), could save more.
